item.title: About
item.content:encoded:
Ben is a staff writer at Risk.net where he writes about credit derivatives and aspects of derivatives markets that impact the buy side. His stories have examined investor responses to changing market structure, impending regulation, and the transition to alternative risk-free rates.

Relying on data to reveal the story and people to fill in the narrative, Ben approaches his coverage by asking what the numbers and the human participants can — and can’t — tell us. While anecdotes are not always representative, data, too, can obfuscate reality in complicated ways; Ben looks to balance the two sources of information and help readers understand the intricacies of the world around them.

Ben's work has appeared in Risk, The Wall Street Journal, the Washington Post, The Times (London), The Real Deal, Norwood News, Inequality.org, as well as the student-publications The Fordham Ram and Fordham Political Review.

Ben received his bachelor's degree from Fordham University, graduating Phi Beta Kappa and majoring in sociology and American studies, and his master's in financial journalism at City, University of London. After growing up on Vermont’s dirt roads, Ben now lives in London and no longer associates “football” with America’s Sunday tradition.

item.title: Intro Data Journalism
item.content:encoded:
Are US PUBLIC pensions really going bust?

By Ben St. Clair

When Illinois experienced fiscal challenges in recent years, commentators and lawmakers echoed a common refrain. The state pension plans were continuing to weigh on public finances and needed reform, they said.

The argument, and the controversy surrounding pension plans, is not unique to Illinois.

“For some states, pensions continue to be a source of budget and credit pressure and usually reflect a history of poor funding discipline,” S&P Global wrote in a 2016 report.

Any discussion of public pensions is bound to draw the attention of the 44 million Americans paying into state and local plans across the country, the 14 million currently receiving benefits, and the numerous private firms managing some of the funds’ combined $4.6trn of assents.

But the story commonly told about the demise and sorry state of public pensions may be overblown — and the truth more nuanced than critics make it seem.

“The narrative of runaway pension obligations sinking an ailing city’s finances is simply not supported by the facts,” writes Tom Sgouros of the Haas Institute for a Fair and Inclusive Society.

So what’s actually going on? The answer lies in a mixture of funding and accounting.

 

Running on a shoestring?

Pension plan liabilities refer to benefits plans expect to pay when members retire. Funds are built up through a combination of government and member contributions and returns on financial investments.

Both maintaining contributions and realising high enough returns to cover benefits can pose challenges for states.

“Adequately funding pension benefits is a challenge for many or most plans,” said Keith Brainard, research director for the National Association of State Retirement Administrators, in a phone interview.

According to Eugene Steuerle, a fellow at the DC-based Urban Institute, politics are partially to blame.

“States are often driven by the same politics as applies to almost all governments: spend now, tax less now, and push some of the burden off to future elected officials and citizens,” he said in an email. “Some give into the temptation more than others.”

States can contribute less to plans if expected investment returns are high and the funding ratio, the gap between current assets and future liabilities, remains low.

Calculating the funding ratio requires making a number of assumptions about future investment returns and the pace at which plans will have to pay retirees. If, in 25 years, a plan expects to pay out $1bn and accounts for a 7.4% annual return, the typical expectation held over the last 16 years by US pension funds, it would need just under $170,000 in assets today to be considered fully funded. If plans are less than “fully funded,” state governments may feel the pressure to make adjustments.

“This practice obscures the true extent of public sector liabilities,” writes Joshua Rauh of the Hoover Institution, a conservative think tank. “The targeted returns may or may not be achieved, but public sector accounting and budgeting proceed under the assumption that they will be achieved with certainty.”

In order to reach high returns (which have mostly failed to reach since 2001), states and cities have turned to alternative investments like private equity, hedge funds, commodities and real estate. The median plan has roughly doubled its exposure to these assets over the last decade, according to an analysis of the Public Plans Database (PPD), which includes data for 170 state and city plans.

Some plans remain more exposed than others. In 2016 the Missouri State Employees pension fund held 62 percent of its $8.8bn assets in alternatives. Georgia’s employee pensions system, on the other hand, held less than one percent of its $29bn assets, among the lowest of pension plans examined.

Alternatives pose a greater risk than bonds, which comprised a large portion of pension funds in the 20th century, but accounting standards allow funds to use expected returns as if they’re guaranteed. The result, Rauh argues, is a funding gap inflated by as much as 170 percent, from $1.4trn to $3.8trn.

“The typical US public pension is run on a shoestring,” write analysts from McKinsey & Company, citing the lack of adequate staffing for the size of the assets under management. With median funding ratios covering roughly three fourths of liabilities in 2016, some may apply the same description to the funds potential to meet future payments.

Like a concentration in alternatives, plan funding ratios vary widely — even within states. But it’s this ratio that critics use to point to “underfunded” plans and a dire future for state retirees.

Thinking differently about pension funding

Other analysts question this line of thinking, however, pointing to the funding ratio’s roots in accounting.

“Although the funding ratio is the most popular and recognised metric of a pension plan’s condition, it is not by itself a reliable indicator of the plan’s condition,” Alex Brown, a researcher with NASRA, said in an email. “Rather, the funding ratio is a ‘point in time’ measurement of a pension plan’s progress toward meeting is long-term funding objectives.”

According to Sgouros, using the ratio to judge a plan’s health fundamentally mistakes the nature of pension liabilities because it assumes that funds will have to immediately make payments to all beneficiaries — an unlikely occurrence.

“Accounting rules imply an equal urgency to all debts, something that is obviously not the case,” Sgouros writes. The only debts that are truly urgent, he argues, are the benefits to pay out each year.

In fact, “under the right conditions, a pension system can pay benefits indefinitely at funding levels much lower than ‘full’ funding,” Sgouros added. As the data show, the combination of investment income and contributions has outpaced required benefit payments in the last 15 years.

In this view, cries of an impending pension crisis are much overblown. Pensions still require proper funding and professionally managed investing teams, but a requirement to fund fully all future liabilities may actually be what is stressing state finance, opponents of the metric contend.

After all, allocating finite tax revenues involves making choices.

“Few government goals can be considered to trump all others, and diversion of taxes into pension savings is a choice not to fund something else,” Sgouros writes.

Author's Notes

The data used in this story is available at publicplansdata.org, and my Excel calculations are available here. For a full explanation of the data and a reflection on my experience writing and reporting the story, click here.

item.title: Intro Data Journalism Reflection
item.content:encoded:
Reflection

Perhaps the hardest part of this assignment was finding a dataset interesting and robust enough to spend hours pouring over. The richness and complexity of the Public Plans Data (with over 260 columns and 2700 rows) made for such a dataset —   fun, and sometimes frustrating, entry into a topic I knew very little about. The attached Excel file (also linked at the end of the article) shows some of the steps I took to clean, organise, and make sense of the data. All columns and rows marked in brown represent my own calculations and analyses, which ultimately went into the piece’s Tableau visualisations. The most complicated step involved combing data from each state’s plans into single entries by state and by year. To compute the data in this way, I used a series of SUMIFS statements to selectively add cells.

To verify the trends and important pieces of data I was identifying, I read a number of reports by think tanks, advocacy groups, and market analysts. I then contacted various researchers to comment on US pensions. Their input added depth and insight to my research. Ultimately, the process models the combination of qualitatative and quantitive reporting I’m looking to do in my career.

item.title: The contentious math behind US and UK pension “crises”
item.content:encoded:
The contentious math behind US and UK pension “crises”

Funding gaps have defined how pension funds and lawmakers behave — for better or worse

As academics from universities across the UK continue to walk out of classrooms and protest  proposed changes to their pension plans, they share what has become a trans-Atlantic concern about the future of retirement schemes.

But their worry has little to do with the so-called funding ratio that shows the critical underfunding of US public pension plans and the Universities Superannuation Scheme (USS) for UK academics. It has to do with the accounting behind that number.

“Although the funding ratio is the most popular and recognised metric of a pension plan’s condition, it is not by itself a reliable indicator of the plan’s condition,” Alex Brown, a researcher with the US-based National Association of State Retirement Administrators, said in an email. “Rather, the funding ratio is a ‘point in time’ measurement of a pension plan’s progress toward meeting its long-term funding objectives.”

The funding ratio compares present asset values to the amount plans anticipate owing retirees in the future. If, in 25 years, a plan expects to pay out $1bn and accounts for a 7.8% annual return, the typical expectation held over the last 16 years by US public pension funds, it would need roughly $150m in assets today to be considered fully funded (assuming it received no further contributions). 

It’s this process of judging a fund’s current health by its ability to meet all future payouts that draws concerns with pensioners. It assumes, they argue, that the fund must be able to continue operating even if the beneficiaries’ business has collapsed. For UK academics, it would mean that UK universities have ceased to exist. 

“USS has the advantage that it doesn’t really need to act like that because there’s pretty much zero chance of the whole sector disappearing,” Sam Marsh of the University of Sheffield said in an interview.

Public pension holders in the US, whose employers include state-wide education systems and city police forces, would agree.

“Under the right conditions, a pension system can pay benefits indefinitely at funding levels much lower than ‘full’ funding,” writes Tom Sgouros of the US-based Haas Institute for a Fair and Inclusive Society. 

The data support this claim. Contributions and investment earnings in US schemes and the USS have largely exceeded benefit payments over the last decade.

But policymakers have seen the fundings gaps as reasons for concern and attempted to close the holes. US states and cities have turned to alternative investments like private equity, hedge funds, commodities and real estate to boost returns — roughly doubling the median plan’s exposure to these assets over the last decade, according to an analysis of data from 170 state and city plans.

The USS has responded by proposing to shift all future plans to a defined contribution model, where the amount received in retirement depends on the fund’s investment returns. Educators say the proposal would leave them worse off in retirement.

But both sides can agree on at least one point: It’s all about the accounting.

item.title: Stabilised but broken
item.content:encoded:
Stabilised but broken

Repairing NYC’s apartments goes deeper than removing rent stabilisation

 

Note: The following piece is a condensed version of my undergraduate thesis on the connection bewteen maintenance conditions and New York City’s rent-regulation system. The thesis was 7,400 words and included over 25 interviews with tenants, owners and members of community organisations. I’m including charts produced with SPSS to show the scope of the piece’s statistical analyses. I consider the work a combined piece of long-form journalism and academic research, and my goal was to tell a story both centred on data and grounded in the lived experiences of those effected.

 

The building’s residents started trickling into the meeting around 7 p.m. For at least one person, who brought an orange plastic stool to sit on, the meeting was nothing new. The rest of us stood around the building’s lobby or sat on the stairs at either side. For the next hour and a half, the residents shared their stories about the building’s maintenance: inconsistent heat and hot water, mould in the bathroom, and a superintendent and landlord who wouldn’t make repairs. 

It was late October 2016, and we were in an apartment building in the South Bronx, several blocks from Yankee Stadium. Back in March, residents had filed a lawsuit against the landlord, citing 238 open violations issued by the city’s housing agency and detailing maintenance issues in 38 apartments — from holes in floors to exposed electrical wires.

The building’s issues were not unique. In 2014, nearly one in five apartments, or over 325,000 units in New York City, experienced three or more maintenance deficiencies. Over 78,000 of these apartments had five or more issues. 

While this building’s residents blamed their superintendent and landlord for the poor maintenance, economists have come to a different conclusion about housing quality in cities like New York. In apartments and buildings like the one I visited, economists point to the large numbers of units subject to rent stabilisation, a distinction that limits the amount landlords can charge each month in rent. 

The narrative goes like this: Without making money from rent increases, landlords do not have the ability or the incentive to make repairs and improvements, so buildings with rent-regulated units fall into disrepair.

With almost all of its apartments under rent stabilisation, the building I visited could serve as an example for what economists have argued.

But according to a statistical model I developed with U.S. Census Bureau data, rent stabilisation is only part of the story. Factors like race and location play a more important role.

In fact, their combined effect on poor maintenance is nearly 70 percent higher than the effect of rent stabilisation alone. Living in that neighbourhood by Yankee Stadium has the highest impact on poor conditions today, 17 percent greater than the impact of stabilised rents.

My finding may not be surprising. Historically speaking, “your apartment is more likely to be in poor living condition if you are black or Latino below a certain income,” said Gregory Jost, former deputy director of the Bronx-based non-profit University Neighborhood Housing Program.

The exact causal mechanisms of location remain unclear, though, and the data leave much unexplained. But the numbers suggest that while it may have been accurate to blame rent stabilisation for the city’s poor maintenance 30 years ago, similar arguments today make increasingly less sense, especially when they’re compared to explanations of race and location. 

A month after I visited the South Bronx apartment, a resident called me and said the conditions in her apartment had not improved. I asked if she had thought about moving. “I’m trying,” she told me. “I’m working two jobs just to get out of here.”

item.title: How Leaving the EU Could Endanger Research Funding
item.content:encoded:
How Brexit Could Endanger Research Funding

When the UK breaks away from the European Union next March, academics worry it may be leaving important research funding opportunities behind.

The £62bn EU research initiative, Horizon2020, has proved lucrative for UK universities, which have nabbed roughly £8bn of funding since 2014, or 28 percent of the funding awarded to higher education. 

“Currently the situation is very good for UK researchers because they can apply for these EU grants,” said Ludovic Highman, a senior research associate at UCL. “What’s not certain at all is the next seven year cycle, and that’s really the most important thing,” he added, referring to the block of EU funding starting after the official Brexit date.

Just months after the Brexit vote, Philip Hammond said the government would guarantee all funding grants awarded before the UK leaves.

But whether or not the UK’s separation from the EU will affect its future access to funding — and its ability to do research — remains uncertain. For some, though, the answer is clear.

“If you pull the plug on a line of funding, which you’re bound to do with Brexit, you’re bound to do less,” said John Dainton, professor emeritus of physics at the University of Liverpool and spokesman for the Council for the Defence of British Universities. “Simple as that.”

Show me the money

If past funding is any indication, Britain’s top universities have the most to lose. Between 2014 and September 2017, Oxford and Cambridge together pulled in £4.5bn in EU research grants, covering over 650 participants. UCL and Imperial College of London were award £2.1bn and £1.5bn, respectively.

Losing funding may impact smaller universities more, said Highman, especially if they receive proportionately more EU grants than larger ones and cannot rely on their size to make up for the lost funding. 

But the sector as a whole will nevertheless feel the loss of EU money.

“What it does is take the infrastructure base for funding and the money base for funding projects back to the levels of the 1970s when we were always struggling to keep up with the rest of the world,” said Dainton.

“It is certainly crippling to some extent British science,” he added. “It can’t compete on a level playing field with France, Germany, Italy and other European countries.”

Funding for research also fuels the UK economy, according to a 2016 report by Universities UK, which represents the country’s higher education institutions. EU research funding adds £1bn to GDP, half of which comes from outside the university sector, and accounts for 19,000 jobs across the country, the report found.

Participation in the funding programs has also not put a burden on the Treasury. Despite contributing £5.4bn to the last seven-year funding cycle, Britain got back roughly £8.8bn.

Publish or perish

Academics have a saying when it comes to research: “Publish or perish.” Journal publications — or the lack thereof — can make or break careers, and one of the key metrics for judging a publication’s success is the number of times other academics cite it. Research shows that papers with international co-authors receive more citations, which is bad news for post-Brexit academia if the UK’s departure means less collaboration.

“You might see that kind of highly cited research output diminish, and that would then in consequence diminish UK universities’ good standing in world rankings,” said Higham

Some researchers aren’t sticking around to find out. “Already we’ve seen the top scientists who came in the last five or six year — an awful lot of them have left the UK,” Dainton said.

Alister Scott of Northumbria University took to Twitter last month to lament one of his colleagues leaving the UK because of possible funding losses. “We cant afford to lose such talented people from our universities,” he wrote.

According to Dainton, European researchers who have collaborated with academics in the UK have been reluctant to let their British colleagues lead projects for fear that it will limit future funding opportunities. The greater loss is one of collaboration and opportunity, he said.

“I would certainly say that among the world of physics, whatever sort of physicist you are whatever sort of engineer you are, everybody sees it as a huge negative,” said Dainton.

Uncertain times

Like many other sectors readying for the impact of Brexit, the source of future research funding remains uncertain. Even with the government’s commitment to fund grants awarded before March 2019, projects initiated after the date may struggle for funding.

“It’s not very clear where the UK government is going to get that extra funding from especially once you have to deal with all other areas when exiting the EU. There’ll be so many competing priorities,” said Higham.

It’s another piece of “Brexit confusion,” according to Jonathan Rokem of UCL who tweeted about the question of research funding.

The UK could still retain access to the next seven-year funding program, but that participation could come with a fee and with limited rights. 

“It is likely that we would be able to apply as an associate country at the least and as a major participant of previous frameworks there is a will to work with the UK on maintaining access,” Richard Wigley of the grant application consultancy GrantTree said in an email. 

“At the moment our advice is to apply while it is still an available funding stream,” Wigley said.

item.title: ICO World
item.content:encoded:
ICO World: Will the hip new fundraising model get over its regulatory hurdle?

While crypto and blockchain evangelicals foresee an end to venture capital, others remain skeptical of the new fundraising model

 

It’s a mad, mad ICO world. Or at least it used to be.

As regulators around the world continue to weigh in on initial coin offerings — the sale of digital tokens as a way for companies to raise money — many decry the attempted government interference in an idea that defies centralisation. Others welcome what they see as a much-needed push to standardise an otherwise beneficial process so far defined by its fraudulent actors.

Whatever the reality, ICOs have proven to be a lucrative form of financing. According to an analysis of funding rounds listed on Crunchbase, a database of global investments, ICOs raised $9.3 billion in 335 global offerings between January 2017 and mid-April 2018.

Other sources put the figure much higher, including a study by Coinbase estimating that offerings in 2018 have already pulled in more that $8 billion.

ICOs are particularly hard to quantify without regulatory filings and consistently reliable reports, but the trend over the last year has been clear.

Crunchbase data shows that there were only three ICOs in 2016, compared to 220 in 2017 and 105 in the first three and a half of months of 2018. Globally since the start of last year, the funding model has attracted the interest of companies in 43 countries.

The question is, are ICOs are here to stay?

 

Security or utility

Unlike shares that give investors a stake in a company’s profits, tokens offer the potential for future use on a company’s platform. The exact nature of offerings vary widely. Some companies offer tokens long before they have a product to show for it while others like the messaging app Telegram do so after developing an established tool. But at their most basic, coin offerings are one of many ways companies can raise money — and do so without the disclosures common in the more traditional venture capital model.

Once they’re offered, tokens often trade hands on the secondary market like many other investments

Those who argue ICOs are separate from securities see them more as donations or buying “utility” in a company’s future product, not an interest in the company itself.

It’s the regulators’ assessments that matter, though. The Securities and Exchange Commission, a US regulator, broadly defines a security as an asset where a third party induces an expectation of future return.

Their stance on ICOs is more conditional, stressing that a token’s use and purpose, not what it’s called, determines whether or not it represents a security. In June the regulator concluded that Bitcoin and Ether, trading on a secondary market and under certain conditions, may not constitute a security. But wrapped up in an investment package, both cryptocurrencies would become securities and fall under existent regulation.

Eitan Jankelewitz, a partner at Sheridans, a London-based law firm, argues ICOs must comply with regulations. He said Sheridans has advised over two-dozen potential coin offerings, but only seen a handful through the offering itself.

“You have to assume that any ICO token is intended to be freely transferable,” said Jankelewitz. “Therefore laws that would ordinarily apply to things like public markets, stock exchanges and things — they begin to bite because you have an interest in a company which can be an exchange between different individuals.”

The regulations help guard against fraudulent offerings, which deploy similar strategies as any other investment scheme, Jankelewitz said.

But fraudulent ICOs are not hard to spot, according to David Yermack, chair of the finance department at New York University.

The legitimate ICOs disclose a good amount of information about their business, he said, relaying his findings as part of an upcoming paper, in order “to signal to the market that they have a good business plan, a good track record”.

Yermack questions whether regulators like the SEC should have to police coin offerings at all, but the SEC’s ongoing position suggests they see the possibility of a future role.

How palatable coin offerings become to regulators may decide whether the ICO money machine keeps rolling, according to Philip Young, marketing director for the Gibraltar Stock Exchange, which also provides a venue to trade tokens. At a small London blockchain event in May, Young told his audience that the sector’s innovation needed to extend beyond the technology.

“You’ve got to think about ethical innovation as well,” he said. “Really creating standards for us as a community to grow up and create a better marketplace — to change it from what it is at the moment, very much a niche part of the economy, to something that should become mainstream.”

item.title: Blockchain Pivots
item.content:encoded:
Companies show mixed success after pivoting to blockchain

Name changes and blockchain acquisitions have proved hit or miss for companies and their shareholders

 

No company wants to be left behind by new technology. So with the rise of blockchain and cryptocurrencies, some businesses were presented with an opportunity they found too good to resist.

Since the two words entered the public’s lexicon last year, a number of companies have looked to attach blockchain to their work, regardless of whether or not they previously used it — or even dealt with digital technology at all.

In a space often likened to a wild west environment, some of these companies have chosen to navigate the blockchain and cryptocurrencies landscape while already beholden to regulatory filings and shareholder pressure, unlike their startup peers that work more independently.

The companies have done so with mixed success. All 10 of the public companies examined for this report saw their shares rise after announcing they would change their name and pivot to blockchain. Six maintained a higher share price after 120 days of trading, and the others saw their shares decline, sometimes dramatically.

(The analysis did not take into account fluctuations in outstanding shares, which could have diluted or inflated each share’s value.)

Online Blockchain experienced one of the more successful pivots. The UK-based company, formerly known as Online Plc, saw its shares rise and fall sharply before reaching a peak 50 days after the company changed names in October.

Shortly after, the company increased its shares by 13 percent, raising £1 million in the process, diluting its current shareholders and possibly leading to a fall in share price.

With its creation of cryptocurrencies PlusOneCoin and Brazio, a coin specific to the Brazilian market, the company may be exposed to the rise and fall of the general crypto market.

The exposure would match the company’s assertions that its name change reflects a legitimate business pivot, which they had taken well before announcing the change.

“OBC is bulding [sic] a company on strong fundamentals to develop businesses based on Blockchain,” a representative for the company said in an email. “Their focus is on user cases of blockchain applications not riding on hype of crypto or technology.”

Another UK firm, Blockchain Worldwide, formerly Stapleton Capital, and Vancouver-based Hive Blockchain Technologies, formerly Leeta Gold Corp, have each maintained high share prices since their announced pivot. Hive’s share price reached nearly 10 times its previous price after 120 days of trading.

To the market at least, six of the 10 companies examined have made the pivot successfully.

 

Unsuccessful pivots

While companies pivot operations for a number of reasons, doing so during one of the largest bull runs in history can pose challenges.

Using blockchain successfully requires matching the variations in the technology’s design to its existing architecture, said Anja Bedford, who helps lead Deutsche Bank’s blockchain efforts. A hard pivot without laying previous groundwork may take time to establish shareholder value, or any value at all.

Take Nodechain, for example. Founded in 2013 and formerly known as Alpine 2 Inc, the company changed its name in 2014 to Vapetek Inc before pivoting to blockchain and changing its name again in December. Currently a two-person company, Nodechain holds a market cap just over $2 million.

Their blockchain bump wasn’t immediate, as their shares remained flat until later in December when the company disclosed its purchase of five computers equipped for mining cryptocurrency. In the same announcement, Vapetek said it had ceased operating its e-cigarette and vapour business and planned to sell all related assets.

Over the next two days, the California-based company saw its shares increase 300 percent. But within three months, the price had dropped to less than a third of what it had been worth before the name change, settling 120 trading days later at two percent of its former value.

In the company’s annual report, made public in April, its independent auditor wrote that Nodechain needed additional financing and a sustainable and profitable businesses model to continue operations into the future.

“The ability to successfully resolve these factors raise substantial doubt about the Company’s ability to continue as a going concern,” the auditor concluded.

Nodechain did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Long Island Iced Tea met a similar fate. A day after changing its name to Long Blockchain in December, shares for the sugary beverage company rose 270 percent.

“We view advances in blockchain technology as a once-in-a-generation opportunity, and have made the decision to pivot our business strategy in order to pursue opportunities in this evolving industry,” then chief executive Philip Thomas said in a statement at the time.

The company said it was in the initial stages of “evaluating specific opportunities involving blockchain technologies”.

But from there the company’s position trended downward: it replaced Thomas in February and announced it would spin off its beverage business. In April NASDAQ suspended the company’s shares from trading on the exchange because of Long’s failure to maintain the minimum market capitalisation.

(Long had previously received suspension notices months before it changed its name, leading some to speculate that their shift to blockchain was an attempt to boost their shares.)

The company’s shares moved to over the counter markets and their price continued to decline, falling to roughly 15 per cent of their value before the company changed names.

Long Blockchain, too, did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

item.title: Blockchain Jungle
item.content:encoded:
Navigating the blockchain jungle

Defining blockchain technology is less important than matching its various designs to real business needs

 

Blockchain’s biggest threat sits in a one-room office in a London co-working space. Or so they would have you believe. The company, Radix, has yet to launch publicly and has only the statistics from internal tests to demonstrate their innovation. But they claim their product will reinvent the technology landscape: “Blockchain, your days are numbered,” reads the slogan visible on a large display board in their office.

Radix, which draws its name from the Latin for “root”, is in many ways indistinguishable from other technology startups. They have a sharp-looking website with links to whitepapers explaining their product design. They operate a channel on the messaging app Telegram to promote their work and answer questions from potential future users. Their code-obsessed founder is controversial, and some argue the company is nothing more than a scam. They may have potential, but they’re entirely unproven.

In other words, they’re the typical blockchain company — just don’t call them that. Radix’s chief operating officer, Robert Olsen, says they don’t have a blockchain. They don’t mine currency, require obscene amounts of energy to operate, or even use blocks. “What we bring to the table is massive scalability, stability and sustainability,” said Olsen, rattling off Radix’s features like a sales pitch he’s given dozens of times.  

As other companies work to assert their connection to blockchain technology and benefit from the attention, Radix has looked to separate itself from the term. Their claims raise the question of what it means to be a blockchain company and to utilise the innovation. 

“To this day there is no accepted definition of what a blockchain is. There is no standard,” according to Anja Bedford, who helps lead Deutsche Bank’s blockchain efforts.

Indeed, the line between blockchain, a distributed digital ledger, and a traditional database is hazy at best, and many definitions rely on the blockchain design used to support Bitcoin, which has few applications outside the cryptocurrency. 

The continuum between new blockchain technology and its alternatives is further complicated by the fact that most, if not all, of the technology that makes up a blockchain design was created decades earlier.

“As people have tried to take that technology and apply it, it has mutated incredibly,” Martin Walker of the Centre for Evidence-Based Management told Parliament in May. “It is almost meaningless to talk about blockchain as a single technology, because it is not anymore.”

The resulting fragmentation of blockchain designs poses challenges not only for those trying to understand it but also for those looking to incorporate it into their business, especially when they see blockchain as the ultimate fix-all solution, Walker said.

How organisations define blockchain becomes less important than figuring out how they plan to implement it and the problems they’re looking to solve.

Using the technology correctly can help companies manage data more efficiently, but misusing it can create unnecessary complexity. “It's a tool and you either use it properly or you don’t,” said Michael Zargham, founder and chief executive of California-based BlockScience. “And like any other tool, you can always invent an example of a thing that doesn't make sense.”

But, Zargham said, “that doesn’t mean it wont change the world”.

 

Genesis block

The original blockchain was used to support the cryptocurrency Bitcoin by keeping track of transactions bewteen users and mark ownership of each coin. To do so, transactions are listed on digital pages (blocks) that some users (miners) validate roughly every 10 minutes by solving computational problems. The user who solves the problem the fastest submits their solution to the network, which in turn comes to a consensus to verify the miner’s work (proof of work) and adds the block to the larger chain. Each block references the one before it — all the way back to the original, genesis block — so changing the chain becomes increasingly more challenging as the ledger grows.

The Bitcoin blockchain supports a self sustaining network, as the currency gets created and rewarded to miners when they add blocks, so basing a definition of blockchain on its first use can be limiting.

Instead, operators have broken the Bitcoin blockchain into its components, listing those as defining blockchain features.

“You don't need a chain, you don't need to have specific blocks, or you don’t really need to have a proof of work or any coins or tokens in that case,” according to Steven Wang, who works on blockchain research at RBS. “The minimum requirement is the network really, a decentralised network.”

Wang’s definition relates to the distributed aspect of the disturbed ledger. Unlike more traditional database designs that locate the authoritative copy in a central location, the Bitcoin blockchain distributes the records to all nodes in the network so each holds a complete copy. Proponents argue decentralisation makes the network more secure.

But according to Zargham, full public distribution is irrelevant since blockchains can exist within  organisations. His blockchain definition includes a system of rules for changing and agreeing on the official state of the ledger — the consensus mechanism and the system’s governance structure.

Bitcoin’s blockchain requires a majority of nodes to agree on the valid ledger each time a miner proposes the next block. Because access to the Bitcoin network is permissionless, anyone can open a node and download the blockchain. The governance design allows for so-called trustless actors, those who have never met or may have competing interests, to come to an agreement on the state of the ledger. 

At its most basic, blockchain remains a data structure, a way of storing information much like the commonly used SQL or JSON designs. 

“It's more in that way down in the weeds tier of technology,” said Zargham, who compares blockchain to a motor controller in mechanical devices.

Paolo Tasca, executive director at the UCL Centre for Blockchain Technologies in London, agrees, referring to blockchain as “a foundational technology”.

“It will have an impact on the architectural infrastructures of our systems that we are using,” he said. 

 

Blockchain jungle

The foundational aspect of the technology — and its amorphous definition — means that the design landscape has fragmented into various blockchain and alternative blockchain designs. Tasca calls this environment “a jungle of different blockchain architecture”.

The variations mean that a blockchain’s specifications must be paired with a specific business system and wont simply solve problems across the board.

“At the end of the day blockchain is just a technology, and you've got to figure out with smart contracts how you can actually apply it and what the business logic is behind it,” said Bedford, referring to the automated agreements run in conjunction with a blockchain.

While Bitcoin continues to run on the same model, other blockchains have shifted away from its proof-of-work verification because of its slow speed and high electricity requirements, globally estimated to consume more energy per year than Switzerland.

Tendermint and Ethereum’s Casper utilise a proof-of-stake model in which miners are determined by the size of their coin holdings. The idea is that those with the largest stake in the system will be less likely to corrupt it.

However, a proof-of-stake fault control risks concentrating mining with a few users, who, depending on how the network is constructed, could remain anonymous. 

Proof-of-authority, on the other hand, could identify those central users who may exert more control over who has access to the network. 

In R3’s Corda, which was developed specifically for use in the financial industry, an authority node grants others permission to read and write into the blockchain, and only those nodes participating in a transaction are aware of the details. The governance model eschews the Bitcoin dream of disintermediation, but proves more suitable for banks and other organisations looking to protect their data and comply with regulations. 

The question then is the degree of centralisation that disqualifies a network design from being considered a blockchain — or if that distinction even matters.

In these more centralised models, the need for a currency to incentivise nodes to participate becomes less relevant, especially if all users have a non-financial reason for being involved — either because they all belong to the same organisation or have an interest in jointly using a blockchain. 

Thus as the organisations move away from a Bitcoin-styled network, the system starts to look less and less like the original blockchain. 

Bedford considers these centralised designs to be more akin to distributed ledgers than actual blockchains. Choosing the right centralisation model depends on the business problem a company is looking to solve.

“If you decentralise something you need a good reason because it slows things down. It adds complexity in a way,” said Eitan Jankelewitz, a partner at Sheridans, a London-based law firm. “I think if you have a genuine use case for decentralisation, blockchain is excellent.” 

A closed blockchain within an organisation could also make sense to address specific data problems.

“It could be [useful] because you're all in the same company, but you have a 100,000-person company with thousands of different database systems and you need to build an accounting and reconciliation system that bridges across silos that are not currently well reconciled,” said Zargham.

But even within a company or consortium of companies, it may be hard sometimes to see the difference between a distributed ledger and its subset distinction of a blockchain. “Especially where you have high trust and aligned interests, you don't need blockchain,” said Bedford. “You can actually run a normal distributed ledger.”

Ultimately, the blockchain’s definition lies on a continuum of technologies; it forks in various directions depending on the exact application. Purists may have their own strict requirements, but with the lack of industry standards, pinpointing an exact definition can be challenging.

 

Reinventing the blockchain

The fragmented blockchain landscape shows little sign of consolidating without industry standards, especially as businesses continue to experiment with the technology.

“Fundamentally I would expect every company will have a whole bunch of internal blockchains,” said David Yermack, chair of the finance department at New York University. “So there wont be hundreds or even thousands but probably millions in the same way that there are millions of accounting ledgers.” 

Radix is hoping to be the foundational technology behind those ledgers. Even as they argue their product is not a blockchain, the company is targeting problems others say blockchains can solve, like handling data from the likely influx of internet-of-things devices. 

Their protocol relies on a design called sharding, in which nodes contain only a piece of the entire ledger and communicate with other nodes to verify transactions. The process makes the system “linear scalable,” according to Olsen, meaning that transaction volume increases with each node added to the system.

Those defining distributed ledger technologies with a broad stroke may still consider Radix a blockchain. 

But the exact definition may be less important than the story behind it and how companies intend to use the technology.

Radix’s narrative is one of reinvention, but their pitch may not work for all companies looking to adopt the technology, or all developers working in the space.

One developer said in an email the “project is a scam at best”, referring to the company’s claims as “smoke and mirrors” and its founder as a fraud.

“Disregard any project that makes scalability claims without being live for at least 1+ years with real usage,” the developer added.

Olsen said the criticism has been constant over the years and compared the skepticism with their founder, Dan Hughes, with that held for Ethereum’s founder, Vitalik Buterin. “There's nothing I know about that would make me question his authenticity,” Olsen said.

Radix launches its alpha product in June before it opens publicly by the end of the year. By then, the narrative driving blockchain development and how companies make use of the technology may have changed dramatically. 

The key, according to Bedford’s explanation of Deutsche Bank’s strategy, is to stay on top of the developments even if you’re not the ones leading the field. 

In a quickly changing jungle, it’s about not getting left behind.

item.title: Banking on blockchain
item.content:encoded:
Banking on blockchain

The technology associated with cryptocurrencies looks very different to the banks adopting it

 

When Adam Rizvi tried to make a Bitcoin transaction in December, Barclays froze his accounts. He wasn’t able to use them for another 10 days. “No-one (Not the bank manager, bank staff, telephone support team or fraud team) would talk to me about it,” he said in an email.

Since then, Rizvi says he’s used another UK bank to make cryptocurrency transactions and through his company, Crypto Bates Group, recommends that his clients do the same.

Even as Barclays very publicly experiments with blockchain technology, which underlies many cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, its position towards the digital currencies has remained muted. In March the bank allowed a UK subsidiary of Coinbase, a San Fransisco-based cryptocurrency exchange, to open an account with its own subsidiary.

But the connection is more “arm’s length” than anything, according to Robert Olsen, chief operating officer of the UK-based, blockchain-like company Radix. “The minute you say blockchain, the banks are like ‘ahh,’” he said, later adding he plans to use a Luxembourg-based bank to open an account.

When reached for comment, a spokesperson for Barclays referred to Vice Chairman Jeremy Wilson’s comments in February 2017 as the company’s “public position on blockchain”.

“I don’t think I’ve ever heard it mentioned in Barclays or in the Whitechapel Think Tank that blockchain is anything other than a significant opportunity for the banks. And not just for the incumbents, but for everyone,” Wilson said at the time.

Others, however, criticise the banking industry’s current use of the technology.

“Banks hate blockchains, they'll never adopt them. They want a blockchain that isn't a blockchain,” Matthew Di Ferrante, founder at Zero Knowledge Labs, said in an email.

Anja Bedford, who helps lead Deutsche Bank’s blockchain efforts, calls the criticism “unheeded”, pointing to the precautions banks are required to take. A breach in a bank similar to those seen in cryptocurrency exchanges would mean “that bank is finished,” Bedford said. “We have to safe keep your data, and we have to comply with regulation,” she added.

Deutsche Bank, too, has been experimenting with blockchain technology. Like Barclays’ bifurcated stance on blockchain and cryptocurrencies — adopting and experimenting with the technology internally while distancing itself from other aspects — their position reflects the challenges many banks face balancing the existing regulatory framework and the desire to innovate with a technology that eschews centralisation and identification.

The challenges mean that when banks talk about using blockchain, they’re referring to a different type of blockchain than what is commonly understood, which has been defined largely by impressions of the Bitcoin network. To more blockchain purists like Di Ferrante, the changes may negate blockchain’s innovations.

But many banks and financial services firms remain optimistic about their use of blockchain and maintain that it will have a transformative impact on the industry.

“If there's going to be an innovation or revolution in banking services, I'm sure that the banks will be ahead of it, and we will just change the way we serve customers,” said Steven Wang of RBS.

The question remains how that changed industry will look.

 

Misplaced innovators?

 

Banks aren’t necessarily known as chief innovators, tending instead to supply funding to or buy up those that do the work. With blockchain potentially threatening the financial industry, though, banks have attempted to adapt the technology to their business.

Blockchain, also known as distributed ledger technology or simply DLT, is difficult to define. While still a nascent development, the community remains fraught with disagreements over what, exactly, constitutes a proper use of the technology.

At its core, though, blockchain is a database structure distributed over various locations. Its entries are cryptographically secured and linked to previous transactions, forming a mostly immutable chain. Depending on its design, all users can edit and write to the blockchain, or receive permission to do so, and the system includes a method for users to come to an agreement about the legitimate state of the ledger.

To the technology’s evangelicals, blockchain is set to change everything from supply chain management and cross-border payments, to medical record storage and personal identification. But some doubt banks are positioned well to lead these innovations, especially compared to newer startups.

“I think if we see it take off, we're going to see it take off in something lower risk and something which is inherently more innovative,” said Eitan Jankelewitz, a partner at Sheridans, a London-based law firm. “Financial services are neither of those things,” he added.

Michael Zargham, CEO and founder of California-based BlockScience, also doubts that banks will be the testing ground for revolutionary blockchain developments. But, he thinks, they have come to understand the technology and attempted to apply it to their work.

“Banks are going to do bank things,” he said. “That's fine, but it's a form of backward innovation.”

When it comes to “bank things” and making an impact on the financial industry, the traditional firms might have an advantage, especially when it comes to navigating existing regulation.

“I'm not sure whether this is the best place, but I would think that this is a safe place to do innovation,” said Wang.

“They [the banks] have a history of knowing how to keep technology safe in terms of privacy issues, in terms of customer identity, in terms of keeping within the limits of legal and ethical constraints,” he added.

 

Banking solutions

 

If anything, blockchain developments may have forced financial institutions to re-evaluate their present data systems. But blockchain technologies do not necessarily work for all information stored in databases, said Bedford.

Regardless, a rethink involves a significant departure from the blockchain designs made popular by cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum’s ether. These systems’ appeal lies in their ability to democratise information and mask users’ identities. In effect, cryptocurrency blockchains bring trust into trustless networks, suppling a framework for strangers to be confident in the validity of the ledger.

Neither attribute, publicity or full anonymity (or pseudonymity in the case of networks that identify users by a unique hash) makes sense for banks. With know-your-customer (KYC) and anti-money-laundering (AML) regulations in place, banks are held accountable for the businesses and individuals they serve.

As a result, their blockchains — if you call them that — will come with significant adjustments.

“I think if you are one of the legacy banks you probably cannot use the decentralised model without falling out of compliance with other things, and this is a real cost to them,” said David Yermack, who chairs the Finance Department at New York University.

“Industry is gravitating toward a model where there would be a gatekeeper who would be the monopolist custodian who would have the exclusive right to update the blockchain,” Yermack added.

Corda has been this model and the industry’s solution to its regulatory needs. Developed by R3, which leads a consortium of 200 banks and financial institutions, Corda is a permission-based, blockchain-like protocol developed for business.

“Corda was built by the financial industry, for the financial industry,” write Charles Cooper and Isabelle Corbet in testimony R3 submitted to parliament in May.

The system, which R3 have said is not, strictly speaking, a blockchain, functions as a shared ledger where transactions are visible only to the parties involved. There’s no mining, currency, or broad consensus mechanism outside of the agreement of the parties engaging in a transaction.

“If we wanted to be skeptical, we might say that Corda’s team was set an impossible task – to design a flavor of blockchain that would suit the banks funding R3,” writes Gideon Greenspan, founder and CEO of UK-based Coin Sciences.

In some ways, Greenspan writes, Corda can be seen “as a heroic but ultimately unsatisfactory compromise between the desire of R3’s members to do something blockchainy, and the commercial and regulatory constraints under which they exist.”

Even if a blockchain ends up meeting the visions enthusiasts have predicted, banks will have to do it their own way.

“It will be an iterative process,” said Bedford. Banks will move up to the more innovative applications as they become more feasible.

Bedford said banks have some blockchain-like systems running alongside legacy systems, but are unable to replace the current methods in some cases because of rules mandating that certain securities be issued in paper form and physically held by a central securities depository.

“Some of the other banks, especially JP Morgan, they already have it running, but most of us are kind of in this shadow production phase where basically the system is running parallel because again, too, regulation,” said Bedford.

Major banks have realised, she added, that their current interconnectivity means any blockchain-like solution will involve significant collaboration. Consortia like R3 then become key.

 

Waiting for a changed industry

When it comes to actually instituting blockchain or blockchain-inspired technologies, organisations require a technological and personnel infrastructure capable of maintaining and debugging the network. Jankelewitz doubts that the pool of talented developers is currently sufficient to meet these needs for banks.

“They're not going to swap onto that anytime soon unless they're totally assured that there is the resourcing there to make it work,” he said. “If it can't serve five million people from day one, then it's not going to work for them.”

Regardless of whether or not banks end up instituting “proper” blockchains, the true impact of the technology, or inspired technologies, remains unclear.

“It would be too restrictive to think that the blockchain stuff would be able to change completely entirely the banking processes — or some of the banking processes,” said Paolo Tasca, executive director at the UCL Centre for Blockchain Technologies in London.

“But together with other toolbox like big data technology, machine learning, artificial intelligence and so on, then it could change a lot.”

So what does that mean for the future of banking? Martin Walker of the Centre for Evidence-Based Management remains skeptical that blockchain will actually increase efficiency and see widespread adoption. After all, it’s not yet possible to automate every aspect of the financial industry.

“Simply having a blockchain does not actually get people to update the status of where the payment is,” Walker told Parliament in May.

The critique underscores some of the challenges the industry faces before blockchain-inspired technologies can become widely used — if they do at all. Interoperability, or connecting different blockchain systems together, also poses a challenge for an industry accustomed to keeping its ledgers separate.

Tasca envisions a future in which banks become more of a “data warehouse” where external providers access the information they need about their customers while banks serve more nuanced purposes.

“The banks become simply a tool that allow more flexible, more quick, and less heavyweight operators to offer specific service that serve a specific segment of the market,” Tasca said.

And yet others have been more bullish on the technology’s transformative impact on the financial industry.

Yermack, who considers blockchain to be the most significant innovation since double entry bookkeeping, predicts that retail banking operations will shift away from the industry leaders. The banks, in his view, will disappear slowly, much like the old US airline industry consolidated and changed in the 20th century.

The disruptive blockchain revolution in banking may be a long way off, though. In June the blockchain-like company Ripple said that at the moment, blockchain’s scalability and privacy issues make it unlikely banks will adopt the technology for cross border transactions, one of the more talked about financial applications.

Over the next year Bedford predicts that the industry will continue to see the right, and wrong, business cases for blockchain. Or make the necessary developments.

“You still see this hype with lots of things happening,” said Bedford. “I personally think we will hit this value of disillusionment on the hype cycle, but that's when you see the actual good use cases happening.”
